options.text: Keep production search entries until backup expiry so all storage systems can be deleted simultaneously under one scheduled maintenance action.
options.why: This leaves in-scope active processing untreated.

options.text: Erase every historical artifact immediately, including legally required records, because a customer request takes priority over all retention obligations.
options.why: The confirmed scope includes legally determined exceptions.

options.text: Remove in-scope derived copies under the approved policy, preventing backup restores from reintroducing erased information into active processing.
options.why: Derived artifacts and restore paths remain within scope.

questions.decision: Apply the legally confirmed scope to actual derived copies and restoration behavior; storage format alone does not settle identifiability.

questions.title: Transparent assistance without irrelevant exposure
questions.stem: A government information assistant helps residents interpret public benefits guidance. Users often mistake its generated explanations for official determinations. The system retains sensitive case details for authorized follow-up, and internal prompts include security controls. The team wants meaningful transparency without exposing protected data or relying on a disclaimer as the only safeguard. Which TWO changes BEST address the actual misunderstanding?

options.text: Add a long legal notice at registration and use completion of that step as sufficient evidence that residents understand each generated explanation.
options.why: Registration acknowledgement does not establish ongoing understanding.

options.text: Present a numerical confidence score beside every response and allow users to treat high-confidence explanations as provisional official determinations.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence does not establish authority.

options.text: Publish complete prompts and internal access-control rules to every resident so they can verify exactly how all service decisions are produced.
options.why: This exposes unnecessary internal security material.

options.text: Evaluate whether users understand the distinction in representative journeys, adjusting interface and escalation behavior when misunderstanding persists.
options.why: This tests effectiveness rather than disclaimer presence.

options.text: Identify explanations as assistance, cite applicable guidance and show the official determination or appeal route when a consequential decision is involved.
options.why: This clarifies the service's authority and recourse.

questions.decision: Transparency should explain evidence, authority and recourse, then be tested with users; it need not expose security or private case details.

questions.title: Discovery before accepting an automation promise
questions.stem: A distribution executive requests an AI assistant to reduce order cycle time by half. Warehouse observation shows picking queues, while the proposed assistant improves order-entry speed. Sales managers also disagree about whether customers can approve substitutions automatically. The team has not measured stage timings or exception demand. What should the architect do FIRST before promising a design and delivery estimate that commits to the executive target?

options.text: Accept the cycle-time target and select an orchestration framework that can later incorporate both entry automation and warehouse decision agents.
options.why: Framework choice precedes essential requirements.

options.text: Map the current process and stage bottlenecks with affected teams, establish baseline outcomes and resolve substitution authority before defining the first release scope.
options.why: The value bottleneck and authority remain unestablished.

options.text: Interview only the executive sponsor to confirm the target, then ask sales and warehouse teams to align after the architecture is approved.
options.why: The conflicting operational constraints remain unresolved.

options.text: Prototype automated order entry and estimate the project from its processing speed, treating warehouse capacity as an operational dependency outside scope.
options.why: This could optimize a nonbinding stage.

questions.decision: Structured discovery establishes the real bottleneck and decision authority before a credible scope or outcome commitment.

questions.title: Explain a trade-off with a decision trigger
questions.stem: A retailer must choose between a faster assisted workflow and a more flexible agentic design. The workflow meets current cases and an eight-week deadline; the agent improves exploratory exceptions but needs additional operational testing. Leadership wants a recommendation with a clear reason to revisit it as demand changes. Which TWO elements make the architecture decision record most useful to technical implementers and business sponsors?

options.text: List every framework feature in equal detail and leave the recommendation open until implementation teams agree on their preferred tooling.
options.why: This avoids the required architectural decision.

options.text: Record measurable exception-volume and quality triggers for revisiting the agentic option, with an owner responsible for gathering that evidence.
options.why: This makes reconsideration accountable and evidence-driven.

options.text: State the chosen workflow against current case coverage, deadline and operating risk, with evidence and explicit limitations relative to the agentic alternative.
options.why: This explains why the decision fits current constraints.

options.text: Promise the agentic design will eventually replace the workflow once a newer model is available, without specifying a business or operational threshold.
options.why: Model availability does not establish business need.

options.text: Describe the workflow as the permanent standard so delivery teams can avoid maintaining evidence about future exception demand.
options.why: This blocks justified lifecycle reconsideration.

questions.decision: A useful decision record connects evidence and constraints to a choice, then names the conditions and owner for reconsideration.

questions.title: An SLA dispute about the clock
questions.stem: A partner-facing assistant meets its model-response latency target, yet partners report service violations because authentication, retrieval and tool retries add several seconds. The contract says a useful answer must arrive within five seconds, but the dashboard measures only the generation span. Product and operations disagree over ownership. What is the BEST immediate alignment step before investing in model-level optimization?

options.text: Define user-visible completion and failure semantics, instrument the complete path and assign ownership for the contractual measure.
options.why: This aligns measurement with the agreed service outcome.

options.text: Amend the dashboard label to clarify that it measures model time and leave partner-facing SLA assessment to the integration vendors.
options.why: This leaves the end-to-end obligation unowned.

options.text: Reduce model output length until generation p95 improves enough to offset an estimated average for other stages in the path.
options.why: Estimated averages do not define the contractual tail.

options.text: Report the sum of each component's independent p95 and treat teams whose individual targets pass as compliant with the overall service.
options.why: Summed marginal p95s are not an end-to-end distribution.

questions.decision: Define and own the user-visible SLI first; isolated generation speed cannot resolve a measurement and accountability mismatch.

questions.title: The receiving team needs an operating contract
questions.stem: A research prototype is being transferred to a central platform team. The demo works, but its author manually refreshes documents, interprets failed tool responses and knows which version combinations were evaluated. The receiving team will own production incidents next month. Which TWO artifacts are most essential at handoff to turn this successful demonstration into a service the new team can operate safely?

options.text: Transfer all prior exploratory prompts as an unstructured archive and ask the receiving team to choose the configuration that seems most reliable.
options.why: This leaves evaluated configuration ambiguous.

options.text: Schedule feature expansion immediately after ownership transfer so the receiving team learns the service through implementing additional capabilities.
options.why: Expansion is not a substitute for operating readiness.

options.text: Provide the complete demo recording and presentation slides, letting the receiving team infer operational steps from the successful walkthrough.
options.why: A demo omits the described manual operations.

options.text: Provide tested incident and rollback procedures with named responsibilities, alert routes and a joint rehearsal of the expected operational failures.
options.why: This establishes executable operating ownership.

options.text: Provide versioned deployment and data-refresh contracts, including supported configuration, validation gates and failure-state behavior that the receiving team can exercise.
options.why: This transfers reproducible implementation knowledge.

questions.decision: Handoff requires reproducible configuration and rehearsed operating procedures, not only knowledge that a prototype can succeed.

questions.title: Iteration after a policy revision
questions.stem: A deployed expense assistant has a stable prompt and successful regression suite. Finance introduces a new exception policy affecting one regional office. Engineers propose editing the live prompt immediately because the change is short. The existing release process requires finance validation for policy behavior and operations acceptance for deployment changes. Which lifecycle action BEST incorporates the urgent change without bypassing those ownership boundaries?

options.text: Edit the live prompt and ask finance to review next week's sample, treating short policy edits as documentation rather than release changes.
options.why: Behavior changes still require validation.

options.text: Freeze all policy updates until the next major model upgrade because the current regression suite proves the existing configuration is reliable.
options.why: This preserves outdated policy behavior unnecessarily.

options.text: Ask the model to retrieve the new policy dynamically and remove finance from release approval because retrieval keeps the prompt unchanged.
options.why: A new evidence policy still changes behavior and authority.

options.text: Version the policy change, add region-specific cases and obtain the required policy and operating validation before a controlled release with rollback.
options.why: Urgency can use a controlled targeted change path.

questions.decision: Iteration is governed by behavioral impact and ownership, not the number of edited words or whether the prompt file changes.

questions.title: Resolve the meaning of a requirement
questions.stem: A service sponsor asks for real-time answers from an engineering assistant. Operations interprets real-time as two-second first token; analysts mean completed evidence-backed answers within ten seconds. Safety wants uncertain equipment instructions escalated rather than confidently completed. The team is preparing architecture estimates, and no service definition has been approved. What is the BEST next discovery activity to avoid building against incompatible expectations?

options.text: Facilitate concrete user journeys with sponsors, analysts and safety owners, defining completion, uncertainty and timing acceptance criteria before comparing designs.
options.why: This resolves the contradictory meaning of success.

options.text: Offer separate latency dashboards to each stakeholder and proceed with architecture selection because each group can monitor its preferred interpretation.
options.why: Separate dashboards preserve conflicting obligations.

options.text: Choose the stricter two-second target for every interaction and estimate the largest model configuration that appears able to stream quickly.
options.why: First token and useful completion remain confused.

options.text: Prototype a ten-second completed response and ask stakeholders to accept its timing once they observe the evidence quality in demonstrations.
options.why: A demonstration does not resolve escalation or contractual acceptance.

questions.decision: Translate vague labels into shared observable behavior before architecture commitments; uncertainty behavior is part of the service contract.

questions.title: Expansion after a narrowly successful pilot
questions.stem: A claims triage pilot meets acceptance gates for one product and language. Another business unit asks to reuse it across different products with new decision rules and a higher peak load. Leadership sees the same assistant interface and assumes rollout is a configuration task. Which TWO lifecycle commitments BEST support informed expansion while preserving the evidence from the successful initial pilot?

options.text: Copy the production prompt unchanged and treat the first month's user satisfaction as sufficient validation for the additional product rules.
options.why: Unvalidated rules expose users before readiness evidence.

options.text: Compare the new unit's rules, data rights, workload and risk profile with the validated scope, identifying which prior evidence remains applicable.
options.why: This distinguishes reusable evidence from new assumptions.

options.text: Reset the original pilot metrics because evidence from one unit cannot contribute to any other deployment with different decision rules.
options.why: Reusable components can retain relevant evidence.

options.text: Define new slice and capacity gates with the receiving owners, then perform a controlled expansion whose rollback preserves the original validated service.
options.why: This validates changed scope without destroying the baseline.

options.text: Expand globally once the new unit confirms the interface looks familiar, then use incident frequency to determine whether extra governance is needed.
options.why: Interface similarity does not establish readiness.

questions.decision: Expansion is a scope change; preserve valid evidence and explicitly validate what the new context changes.

questions.title: Communicating uncertainty in the executive case
questions.stem: An AI sales assistant reduces measured drafting time by 40% in a volunteer pilot. Participants are experienced users, complex deals were excluded and revenue effects have not matured. Leadership asks whether the company should announce a 40% productivity increase across sales next quarter. What should the architect communicate to make the decision useful without understating the demonstrated drafting improvement or overstating the business evidence?

options.text: Report no benefit because revenue effects are not yet known, withholding the drafting result until the next full sales cycle ends.
options.why: This discards a valid measured intermediate gain.

options.text: Estimate total sales productivity from assistant-generated word count and combine it with the drafting gain to strengthen the investment case.
options.why: Word count is not overall business productivity.

options.text: Forecast a 40% productivity gain for all sales staff, adding a confidence disclaimer to acknowledge that the pilot involved experienced volunteers.
options.why: A disclaimer does not justify extrapolation.

options.text: Report drafting gains with pilot limitations, distinguishing total productivity and proposing representative downstream-outcome validation before broader claims.
options.why: This states supported results and the missing evidence.

questions.decision: Communicate measured benefits at their actual scope and maturity, then identify the evidence needed for broader claims.

questions.title: A lifecycle contract for retrieval updates
questions.stem: A platform team receives a knowledge assistant whose source owners publish policy revisions independently. The platform owns uptime, while policy teams own correctness; nobody owns indexing freshness or failed refresh recovery. During handoff, all teams agree the model behaves correctly on the current index. Which TWO additions are required to make ongoing correctness and operations responsibilities concrete rather than relying on this one-time validation?

options.text: Ask policy owners to notify users manually after every revision and consider those notices sufficient to cover indexing delays.
options.why: Users still receive stale assistant evidence.

options.text: Document version lineage and rollback or withdrawal behavior so invalid policy updates can be contained without losing the last validated evidence set.
options.why: This makes updates reproducible and recoverable.

options.text: Define source-to-index freshness expectations, validation checks and an owner for failed or partial refreshes, including alert and escalation routes.
options.why: Freshness becomes an owned operating obligation.

options.text: Transfer model tuning ownership to operations because a correct current index establishes that future correctness failures will be model related.
options.why: Future source and indexing failures remain possible.

options.text: Schedule a quarterly accuracy survey without retaining source or index versions so teams can focus on user outcomes rather than implementation detail.
options.why: The survey cannot diagnose or recover specific invalid updates.

questions.decision: Correctness depends on an ongoing data lifecycle; handoff must assign freshness, validation, version lineage and recovery responsibilities.

questions.title: Team policy versus local preference
questions.stem: A development organization configures Claude Code for several repositories. Teams need shared coding conventions, but production deployment commands must remain subject to centrally managed permission controls. One developer proposes placing the deployment prohibition in project instructions and allowing broad shell execution to reduce interruptions. Which setup BEST separates reusable development guidance from enforceable execution policy while retaining useful team customization?

options.text: Version shared project guidance for coding practices and enforce production-action restrictions through managed permissions and appropriately scoped credentials.
options.why: Instructions guide work; permissions enforce capability boundaries.

options.text: Ask developers to acknowledge the deployment policy at session start, then retain unrestricted credentials for occasional approved production work.
options.why: Acknowledgement does not constrain the available authority.

options.text: Put deployment restrictions into every repository instruction file and let local developers grant broad shell permissions when they understand the guidance.
options.why: Local permission can bypass the instructed prohibition.

options.text: Remove project guidance and encode all style conventions as shell deny rules so every development requirement uses one enforcement mechanism.
options.why: Permission rules do not express coding conventions well.

questions.decision: Use project instructions for conventions and managed permission/credential boundaries for prohibited operations; each serves a different function.

questions.title: Improve the complete engineering workflow
questions.stem: A team adopts a coding assistant and sees pull requests produced faster. Review time increases because generated changes are broad, tests are often unrelated and maintainers struggle to understand design intent. Release lead time is unchanged. The team wants useful productivity rather than more generated code. Which workflow change BEST addresses the observed bottleneck while preserving maintainers' responsibility for the codebase?

options.text: Increase the assistant's parallel coding sessions and count completed pull requests per engineer to reflect the improvement in generation throughput.
options.why: More output can worsen the review queue.

options.text: Scope reviewable changes with explicit acceptance checks, measuring review effort and merge lead time alongside coding time.
options.why: This targets the downstream review bottleneck.

options.text: Require longer generated explanations and complete snapshots of changed files so reviewers receive more material with every pull request.
options.why: More material does not ensure focused reviewability.

options.text: Allow the assistant to approve its own changes after passing tests, using maintainer review only for files that recently caused incidents.
options.why: Test success does not transfer maintainer authority.

questions.decision: Optimize the end-to-end delivery process and reviewability, not a local drafting-time metric.

questions.title: A debugging incident with a permission boundary
questions.stem: A coding assistant cannot run a diagnostic script in a staging repository. The script reads synthetic fixtures, but its wrapper also attempts to access a protected credentials path. A managed permission rule blocks the call before execution. Engineers need the diagnostic result quickly and suggest an allow-all hook. Which TWO actions BEST resolve the issue without treating a debugging deadline as permission to bypass managed policy?

options.text: Disable all managed restrictions until the diagnostic finishes and use logs afterward to confirm the assistant made no unwanted accesses.
options.why: Retrospective logs do not preserve the execution boundary.

options.text: Copy the protected credentials into the staging repository so the diagnostic can access them through an already allowed file path.
options.why: This defeats the protected data boundary.

options.text: Reproduce the minimal diagnostic under approved permissions and record the failing wrapper path for the responsible repository owner to correct.
options.why: This restores useful debugging with accountable repair.

options.text: Add an allow decision in a pre-execution hook and assume it overrides the centrally managed deny rule for this incident.
options.why: Managed deny controls are not overridden by an allow hook.

options.text: Inspect the blocked operation and separate the synthetic-fixture diagnostic from credential access, retaining only the capabilities required by the staging investigation.
options.why: This removes unnecessary protected access.

questions.decision: Diagnose the operation that triggers enforcement and remove unnecessary capability; do not use hooks or copied secrets to bypass policy.

questions.title: A quality gate that is executable
questions.stem: A repository instructs its coding assistant to run a formatter and targeted tests before proposing a change. During busy periods, the assistant sometimes omits one step, and reviewers discover it later. The checks are deterministic and already available in CI. Maintainers want reliable enforcement without treating conversational compliance as proof. What is the BEST configuration and workflow adjustment?

options.text: Use a second assistant to read the conversation and approve changes when the first assistant describes having run the required checks.
options.why: Conversation review still relies on unverified claims.

options.text: Keep project guidance and enforce existing CI checks, using hooks where useful for earlier local feedback.
options.why: Deterministic gates enforce the requirement independently of prose.

options.text: Expand the instruction file with several reminders and require the assistant to state explicitly that every required check has been completed.
options.why: Repeated claims do not establish actual check outcomes.

options.text: Allow maintainers to bypass CI whenever the assistant generated only a small patch because conversational instructions are clearer for low-risk changes.
options.why: Patch size does not prove required checks passed.

questions.decision: Guidance explains the workflow; existing executable gates establish completion. Hooks can shorten feedback without replacing CI authority.

drills.title: Index release review
drills.stem: Judge each proposal independently: does it meet the stated evidence-publication requirement? No fixed number of Yes answers is implied.

rows.text: Requirement: one approved revision per answer. Proposal: validate a complete new index and atomically activate its revision pointer.
rows.why: A coherent evidence generation prevents mixed revision answers.

rows.text: Requirement: reproduce old answers. Proposal: store only the latest source text, retaining document names for historical citations.
rows.why: Names do not recover the historical evidence version.

rows.text: Requirement: authorized retrieval. Proposal: select documents first and hide forbidden citations only when formatting the response.
rows.why: Unauthorized content must not enter the assistant context.

rows.text: Requirement: detect failed refreshes. Proposal: alert on incomplete indexing with a named owner and continue serving the validated generation.
rows.why: The proposal contains failure and assigns a response.

rows.text: Requirement: measure full completion tails. Proposal: use the model first-token histogram as the sole acceptance gate.
rows.why: First token is different from complete response latency.

drills.title: Value and oversight judgments
drills.stem: Judge whether each inference follows from the stated evidence, independently of the other rows.

rows.text: A pilot releases staff capacity while staffing is unchanged; the released hours alone establish equivalent immediate payroll savings.
rows.why: Capacity and cash expenditure are different outcomes.

rows.text: A larger model improves a difficult slice; evaluating routing errors is necessary before claiming a routed system preserves that benefit.
rows.why: Missed exceptions can prevent the larger model from helping.

rows.text: A human review queue exceeds its deadline; the existence of reviewers alone establishes that oversight remains effective.
rows.why: Review capacity and timeliness constrain effective oversight.

rows.text: A policy and assistant change together; versioned comparable cohorts and independent outcome adjudication strengthen causal interpretation.
rows.why: They make competing explanations and actual outcomes observable.

rows.text: A cache test counts prefix writes and reads; fictional prices can support arithmetic without claiming those are current platform prices.
rows.why: Supplied assumptions define the exercise, not current billing.

drills.title: Choose the missing contract
drills.stem: Select the primary missing contract for each situation. Choices may repeat.

rows.text: A generated answer cites a manual name, but the team cannot identify the manual revision used.
A model sees a procurement record because the service credential is broader than the requesting user.
rows.why: The user access boundary is missing.

rows.text: A correct benchmark is repeatedly tuned until it passes, then presented as untouched release evidence.
rows.why: Optimization has contaminated the claimed holdout.

rows.text: A document refresh fails and neither the source owner nor platform team accepts the alert.
rows.why: An accountable failure responder is missing.

rows.text: An analyst approves one adjustment amount, but a different amount executes under the case-level approval.
rows.why: Approval does not cover the executed operation.
